core: The working definition of cash accounting: recording revenue when cash arrives and expenses when cash leaves, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting (Sections 4.1 and 2.1) and corroborated by CFI
The mechanics: no money, no record — a transaction enters the books only when cash actually moves, with an original example
Who uses it: small businesses with simple operations — the general fit, with no tax rules stated as universal
Cash vs accrual: when things count versus when money moves — the contrast, with accrual accounting referenced as a sibling topic only
The strengths, each named: simple, obvious, and in step with the bank account
The weakness: cash accounting can misstate a period's true performance — the honest note, with an original example
The honest framing: cash accounting is honest about the bank balance and fuzzy about performance — the trade-off
supporting: Under cash basis accounting, transactions such as a sale or purchase are not recorded until there is an exchange of cash (OpenStax Sections 4.1 and 2.1)
Cash basis can delay or accelerate revenue and expense reporting until cash receipts or outlays occur, and cash flows are used to measure business performance in a period (OpenStax Section 4.1)

Cash-basis accounting is permitted for nonprofit entities and small businesses that elect to use it, and CFI states the general fit: cash accounting is allowed for sole proprietorships and small businesses while large businesses typically use accrual accounting (OpenStax Section 2.1; CFI)

Accrual accounting records revenues and expenses in the period earned or incurred regardless of when cash moves, giving rise to the revenue recognition and matching principles (OpenStax Section 4.1; CFI)

CFI's honest note on the weakness: a potential flaw with cash accounting is that it can offer a misleading picture of an entity's financial health, especially when unpaid expenses or outstanding receivables are not represented in the financial statements (CFI)

claims.claim: Cash accounting records revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid — under cash basis accounting, transactions such as a sale or purchase are not recorded in the financial statements until there is an exchange of cash.

Cash basis accounting sometimes delays or accelerates revenue and expense reporting until cash receipts or outlays occur, and with this method cash flows are used to measure business performance in a given period.

Cash basis accounting reflects when payments are received and made, not necessarily the time period that the transactions affect — OpenStax's summer-landscaping illustration shows the cash-basis income statement tracking the checking-account balance.

Cash basis accounting is permitted for nonprofit entities and small businesses that elect to use this type of accounting; CFI states the general fit in the same spirit — cash accounting is allowed for sole proprietorships and small businesses, while large businesses will typically use accrual accounting.

Accrual accounting records revenues and expenses in the accounting period in which they are earned or incurred regardless of when cash moves, and gives rise to the revenue recognition principle and the expense recognition (matching) principle — the contrast that defines cash accounting.
Cash basis accounting can be simpler to track than accrual basis accounting, and the cash-basis records mirror the bank account because every recorded item moved through it.

A potential flaw with cash accounting is that it can offer a misleading picture of an entity's financial health, especially when transactions like unpaid expenses or outstanding receivables are not represented in the financial statements — the honest note about misstating a period's true performance.

The honest framing: cash accounting is honest about the bank balance and fuzzy about a period's true performance — the trade-off that explains why it fits small businesses with simple operations and why larger or more complex businesses typically use accrual accounting.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which method is better — cash accounting or accrual accounting?
positions: CFI states that accrual accounting is generally preferred to cash accounting and that cash accounting can offer a misleading picture of an entity's financial health.
OpenStax notes that cash basis accounting can be simpler to track than accrual basis accounting, and that some nonpublic companies may choose to use it rather than accrual.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the choice as a fit-based trade-off rather than a contest: cash accounting is simple, obvious, and in step with the bank account, while accrual accounting gives the fuller picture of performance. Neither method is universally right, and the lesson asserts no universal tax rule — the general fit for small businesses with simple operations is stated as a general fit, not a requirement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does cash-basis profit measure a period's true performance?
positions: Under cash accounting, profit for a period is simply cash received minus cash paid, and work done but unpaid or bills owed but unpaid are invisible until money moves.
The same numbers can flatter or punish a period unfairly when receivables and payables straddle the period boundary, even though nothing in the records is wrong.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the weakness directly, grounded in CFI's flaw note about unpaid expenses and outstanding receivables not being represented in the financial statements, and frames it as the deliberate trade-off of the method: honest about the bank balance, fuzzy about performance. No claim is made that either view is wrong — both describe the same records.
